title: Overclock: building an offline reactor game around an unreliable oracle with AI assistance
author: Optimal_Manner359
selftext:
I’m the creator/publisher of Overclock through Maha Strategies. This is a commercial game showcase, with development assisted by Codex.



The game is about making a stopping decision with imperfect information. PUSH increases your reactor’s unbanked output but can trigger a cascade. BANK saves the pot and ends the round. VERIFY reveals the actual risk and restores some reliability to the oracle. Its displayed risk can drift away from the real probability, especially after ignored BANK warnings. Standard runs last five rounds; points you have already banked stay safe.



Here is the idea in 19 seconds: the oracle displays 15% risk, VERIFY exposes 61%, and pushing anyway loses the 540-point pot: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nxVmrgWYvQA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nxVmrgWYvQA)



For the build, the browser demo became a bundled Capacitor mobile app using Vite. AI assistance covered implementation, tests, release preparation and promotional material. Gameplay runs locally; the oracle is a game mechanic, not a live LLM call. The challenge was keeping displayed forecasts separate from the actual risk while making failures understandable. Seeded outcomes let the same decisions be replayed in testing instead of treating a lucky run as evidence that the logic works.



The mobile work also required checking saved-run restoration after closing the app, native sharing, and the store purchase boundary. Premium is a RevenueCat-backed store entitlement, rather than a local unlock switch. Browser billing mocks help test UI flows but do not establish that real purchases work.



Android: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.mahastrategies.overclock](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.mahastrategies.overclock)



The core game is free, offline and ad-free, with unlimited standard runs, a daily reactor and three campaign scenarios. Optional one-time Premium adds scenarios, governors, custom runs and decision logs (US base $4.99, localized prices vary). No subscription.



I’d like to hear how others test games where the interface intentionally gives imperfect information: how do you distinguish an interesting unreliable narrator from a player simply feeling misled?
